meta.titre: Definite Integrals: area, signed area and volumes of revolution

source.epreuve_titre: GCE A/L Pure Mathematics with Statistics past paper (Cameroon)

sections.contenu_markdown: A potter in Foumban shaping a vase on a wheel produces a solid whose width changes smoothly from base to neck, and a builder in Douala estimating the concrete for a curved wall also meets a quantity made of thin slices of changing size. A definite integral is the exact tool for adding such slices between two limits. At A Level, definite integrals appear regularly, both as short evaluations and volume-of-revolution questions in Paper 1 and as longer 'show that' questions in Paper 2.

items: If $F'(x)=f(x)$ then $F$ is an antiderivative of $f$; standard results include $\int x^{n}\,dx=\dfrac{x^{n+1}}{n+1}+c$ for $n\ne-1$, $\int\dfrac1x\,dx=\ln|x|+c$ and $\int e^{kx}\,dx=\dfrac{e^{kx}}{k}+c$.
The chain rule and the product rule of differentiation, which are reversed in substitution and in integration by parts.
A curve $y=f(x)$ meets the $x$-axis where $f(x)=0$, which is found by factorising.

sections.titre: Evaluating definite integrals, areas and volumes of revolution
sections.contenu_markdown:
**Definition.** If $F$ is an antiderivative of $f$, the definite integral of $f$ from $a$ to $b$ is $F(b)-F(a)$, written $\Big[F(x)\Big]_a^b$. No constant $c$ is needed because it cancels. Useful properties: $\int_a^b f\,dx=-\int_b^a f\,dx$; $\int_a^c f\,dx=\int_a^b f\,dx+\int_b^c f\,dx$; $\int_a^b kf\,dx=k\int_a^b f\,dx$.

### Area
When $f(x)\ge0$ on $[a,b]$, the area enclosed by the curve, the $x$-axis and the lines $x=a$ and $x=b$ is $\int_a^b f(x)\,dx$. Where the curve is **below** the axis the integral is negative, but an area is positive, so use the modulus of that part. If the curve crosses the axis between $a$ and $b$, find the crossing points, integrate each piece separately and add the positive areas. When $y_1\ge y_2$ on $[a,b]$, the area between two curves is $\int_a^b (y_1-y_2)\,dx$.

### Volume of revolution
When the region between $y=f(x)$, the $x$-axis and the lines $x=a$, $x=b$ is rotated completely about the $x$-axis, each thin slice becomes a disc of radius $y$ and thickness $dx$, so

$$
V=\pi\int_a^b y^{2}\,dx \tag{1}
$$

The integrand is the square of the **whole** function, and $\pi$ multiplies the integral. This is not $\pi\left(\int y\,dx\right)^{2}$. Expand any bracket such as $(4x-x^{2})^{2}$ before integrating.

### Techniques met in definite integrals
For a linear bracket, $\int (px+q)^{n}\,dx=\dfrac{(px+q)^{n+1}}{p(n+1)}$ when $n\ne-1$. For a product, integration by parts gives

$$\int_a^b u\,\frac{dv}{dx}\,dx=\Big[uv\Big]_a^b-\int_a^b v\,\frac{du}{dx}\,dx.$$

In every method, keep the limits attached to the variable they belong to.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When the integrand contains a function together with a multiple of its derivative.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Choose $u$, write $du=u'(x)\,dx$ and **change the limits** into values of $u$, so that no return to $x$ is needed. Example: $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin x\cos^{2}x\,dx$ with $u=\cos x$ and $du=-\sin x\,dx$. When $x=0$, $u=1$; when $x=\frac{\pi}{2}$, $u=0$. The integral becomes $\displaystyle\int_1^0(-u^{2})\,du=\int_0^1u^{2}\,du=\dfrac13$.

variantes.nom: Area between a curve and a line
variantes.quand_utiliser: When a region is bounded by two graphs rather than by an axis.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Equate the two equations to find the intersections, decide which graph is higher between them (test one point), and integrate top minus bottom. Example: $y=x^{2}$ and $y=2x$ meet where $x^{2}=2x$, that is $x=0$ and $x=2$. At $x=1$ the line gives $2$ and the curve gives $1$, so the line is higher. Area $=\displaystyle\int_0^2(2x-x^{2})\,dx=\Big[x^{2}-\dfrac{x^{3}}{3}\Big]_0^2=4-\dfrac83=\dfrac43$.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When the integrand is a product such as a polynomial times $e^{x}$, $\sin x$ or $\cos x$.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Take $u$ to be the factor that becomes simpler when differentiated. Example: $\displaystyle\int_0^1xe^{x}\,dx$ with $u=x$ and $\dfrac{dv}{dx}=e^{x}$ gives $\Big[xe^{x}\Big]_0^1-\int_0^1e^{x}\,dx=e-(e-1)=1$. Evaluate the bracket $[uv]$ at both limits before subtracting.

sections.enonce_markdown: The curve $C$ has equation $y=4x-x^{2}$. The finite region $R$ is enclosed by $C$ and the $x$-axis. Find (a) the area of $R$, and (b) the exact volume of the solid formed when $R$ is rotated completely about the $x$-axis.

etapes.justification: These values are the limits of integration, and the sign of $y$ between them shows on which side of the axis $R$ lies.
etapes.resultat_markdown: $4x-x^{2}=x(4-x)=0$ gives $x=0$ and $x=4$. At $x=2$, $y=4>0$, so $R$ lies above the axis.

etapes.action: Set up and evaluate the area.
etapes.justification: Above the axis, the area is the integral of $y$ between the limits.
Use formula (1): square the whole function and multiply by $\pi$.
A squared bracket cannot be integrated directly, so expand it into powers of $x$.
Integrate each power, then subtract the value at $0$ (which is $0$) from the value at $4$.

sections.conclusion_markdown: The area of $R$ is $\dfrac{32}{3}$ square units and the volume of the solid is $\dfrac{512\pi}{15}\approx107.2$ cubic units.

items.pourquoi_faux: The slice is a disc of area $\pi y^{2}$, not $\pi y$. The formula needs the square of the function.
items.correction_markdown: $V=\pi\displaystyle\int_0^4(4x-x^{2})^{2}\,dx$, with the bracket expanded before integrating.

items.pourquoi_faux: The square belongs inside the integral, on $y$. Squaring the value of the integral of $y$ is a different number and has no geometric meaning here.
items.correction_markdown: Square the function, then integrate: $V=\pi\displaystyle\int_0^4 y^{2}\,dx=\dfrac{512\pi}{15}$.

items.pourquoi_faux: After a substitution the limits must be values of $u$, not $x$. The old limits $0$ and $1$ were left in place.

items.erreur_markdown: $\displaystyle\int_0^{2\pi}\sin x\,dx=0$, so the area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $0$ to $2\pi$ is zero.
items.pourquoi_faux: The integral gives a signed total in which the positive half cancels the negative half. An area is never zero here.
The subtraction is in the wrong order: it must be $F(\text{upper})-F(\text{lower})$. A positive integrand over $1\le x\le3$ cannot give a negative integral.

items.enonce_markdown: Evaluate (a) $\displaystyle\int_1^3\left(2x+\dfrac{1}{x^{2}}\right)dx$ and (b) $\displaystyle\int_0^2e^{3x}\,dx$, leaving the answer to (b) in terms of $e$.

(a) Use the substitution $u=x^{2}+16$ to evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^3\dfrac{x}{\sqrt{x^{2}+16}}\,dx$.

(b) Use integration by parts to show that $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi}x\sin x\,dx=\pi$.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) $du=2x\,dx$, so $x\,dx=\frac12du$. When $x=0$, $u=16$; when $x=3$, $u=25$. The integral is $\dfrac12\displaystyle\int_{16}^{25}u^{-1/2}\,du=\dfrac12\Big[2\sqrt u\Big]_{16}^{25}=\sqrt{25}-\sqrt{16}=5-4=$ **$1$**.

(b) Take $u=x$ and $\dfrac{dv}{dx}=\sin x$, so $\dfrac{du}{dx}=1$ and $v=-\cos x$. Then $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi}x\sin x\,dx=\Big[-x\cos x\Big]_0^{\pi}+\int_0^{\pi}\cos x\,dx=\big(\pi-0\big)+\Big[\sin x\Big]_0^{\pi}=\pi+0=$ **$\pi$**, because $-\pi\cos\pi=\pi$.

items.enonce_markdown:
The curve $y=x^{2}-6x$ meets the $x$-axis at the origin $O$ and at the point $P$.

(a) Find the coordinates of $P$ and show that $\displaystyle\int_0^{6}(x^{2}-6x)\,dx=-36$. State the area of the finite region $R$ enclosed by the curve and the $x$-axis.

(b) Find the exact volume of the solid formed when $R$ is rotated completely about the $x$-axis.

(c) Find the value of $k$, with $k>0$, for which $\displaystyle\int_0^{k}(x^{2}-6x)\,dx=0$, and explain the result geometrically.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) $x^{2}-6x=x(x-6)=0$ gives **$P=(6,0)$**. Then $\Big[\dfrac{x^{3}}{3}-3x^{2}\Big]_0^6=72-108=-36$. The curve lies below the axis between $O$ and $P$, so the area is the modulus: **$36$ square units**.

(b) $V=\pi\displaystyle\int_0^6(x^{2}-6x)^{2}\,dx=\pi\int_0^6(x^{4}-12x^{3}+36x^{2})\,dx=\pi\Big[\dfrac{x^{5}}{5}-3x^{4}+12x^{3}\Big]_0^6=\pi\Big(\dfrac{7776}{5}-3888+2592\Big)=$ **$\dfrac{1296\pi}{5}$**, about $814.3$.

(c) $\dfrac{k^{3}}{3}-3k^{2}=k^{2}\Big(\dfrac k3-3\Big)=0$, and $k>0$ gives **$k=9$**. Geometrically, the area below the axis from $x=0$ to $x=6$ (signed value $-36$) is cancelled by an equal area above the axis from $x=6$ to $x=9$, since $\displaystyle\int_6^9(x^{2}-6x)\,dx=\big(243-243\big)-(-36)=36$.

items_markdown: $\displaystyle\int_a^b f\,dx=F(b)-F(a)$: upper limit first, no constant $c$; reversing the limits changes the sign.
Area under a curve is the integral only where the curve is above the axis; split at axis crossings and add the positive areas. Between two curves, integrate top minus bottom.
Volume about the $x$-axis: $V=\pi\displaystyle\int_a^b y^{2}\,dx$. Square the whole function, expand, integrate, then multiply by $\pi$.
In a substitution change the limits into values of the new variable; in integration by parts evaluate $[uv]$ at both limits.
Keep exact forms such as $\dfrac{512\pi}{15}$ or $3\ln5-5\ln2$ until the last line, and only then give a decimal if asked.
